About Velan

Good partnerships begin with the right conversations.

Velan Joint Ventures is presented as a strategic advisory partner for businesses exploring collaboration, joint venture opportunities and new avenues for growth.

Our approach centres on understanding business objectives, clarifying expectations and helping stakeholders evaluate opportunities with a considered, structured process.

  • Understand the business objective and strategic fit
  • Identify partnership needs and evaluation criteria
  • Bring clarity to roles, priorities and next steps
  • Coordinate with appropriate legal and financial professionals when needed

Ask a Specific Question

A joint venture is a business arrangement where two or more parties collaborate on a defined activity or business objective while agreeing how responsibilities, resources, control and returns will be handled.

Business owners, companies, project developers and other organisations exploring a strategic collaboration can submit an enquiry for an initial discussion.

Partner identification may be considered based on the opportunity, target profile, available network and agreed scope. No partner match or outcome is guaranteed.

Commercial discussion points can be organised as part of a structured process. Formal legal advice, drafting and review should be undertaken by appropriately qualified legal professionals.

Start with your company or organisation, sector, broad objective, preferred collaboration type and the stage of your opportunity. Avoid sending confidential documents through an unsecured form.

No business outcome, partner match, funding, return or transaction can be guaranteed. Each opportunity depends on its circumstances, due diligence and decisions by the parties involved.

Technical analysis & expert views

Comparing structures, and what to discuss first.

A general comparison of collaboration models and a discussion checklist. Every deal differs, so treat these as starting points for advisers.

General characteristics of three ways to collaborate (illustrative, not advice)
FactorContractual collaborationEquity joint ventureAcquiring a controlling stake
Separate entityNo, parties stay separateYes, a jointly owned entityNot applicable, the target becomes owned
Level of commitmentLowerMedium to higherHighest
Flexibility to unwindHigherMediumLower
Setup complexityLowerMedium to higherHigher
How control worksSet out in the contractShared through governance rightsMostly with the acquirer

The bars are qualitative indicators only. Entity form, tax and regulatory treatment must be confirmed with qualified professionals.

  • Exit and transfer terms
  • Regulatory approvals

Interactive tool

Joint venture ROI estimator.

Test how your own assumptions play out over time. It is a simple illustration using only the figures you enter. It is not a forecast, valuation or financial advice.

Your assumptions

Example inputs Round numbers pre-filled for illustration only. They are not benchmarks. Replace them with your own.

Capital or asset value you put in at the start.
Revenue attributable to your share, once the venture is running.
Share of revenue left as operating profit.
Extra yearly funding or management cost you carry.
Years before revenue starts. Ongoing cost still applies.
Between 1 and 10 years.
Used for the NPV. Choose a rate that reflects your cost of capital and risk.

Assumptions used

  • Upfront contribution is paid in year 0; all other flows occur at year end.
  • Yearly cash flow = revenue × margin − ongoing cost, with revenue starting after the ramp-up.
  • Simple ROI = net position ÷ upfront contribution. NPV discounts each year at your rate. IRR is indicative and may be undefined.
  • Ignores tax, inflation, exit value, financing and risk. Use qualified advisers for decisions.

Your results

Frequently asked questions

Questions worth asking early.

General information for business leaders, not legal, tax or investment advice.

Related search topics

  • joint venture vs strategic alliance
  • joint venture agreement key terms
  • how to choose a joint venture partner
  • joint venture due diligence checklist
  • joint venture exit strategy
  • joint venture governance structure
  • joint venture feasibility study
  • joint venture risk management

A joint venture usually involves the parties committing resources to a defined business activity and sharing control and returns, often through a separate entity or detailed contract. A strategic alliance is typically looser: the parties cooperate on shared goals while staying independent. The boundary is not fixed, so what matters is what the parties actually agree.

No. Ownership and control can be split in many ways. What matters is that contributions, decision rights, funding obligations and returns are agreed deliberately and are consistent with each party's objectives.

There is no standard timeline. It depends on the complexity of the opportunity, the number of parties, due diligence, regulatory requirements and how quickly the parties align on key terms.

Typical topics include events that trigger an exit, how the venture is valued, transfer restrictions, what happens to intellectual property, staff and contracts, and how disputes are resolved. These terms should be drafted with qualified legal counsel.

Qualified legal, tax and financial professionals should advise on those matters. Velan's role, as described on this website, is to help organise the commercial discussion and coordinate with such professionals where needed.

No. No business outcome, partner match, funding, return or transaction can be guaranteed. Each opportunity depends on its circumstances, due diligence and the decisions of the parties involved.

Home / Industries / Real Estate & Infrastructure
Industry perspective

Real estate and infrastructure joint ventures.

Project collaboration and development opportunities often depend on land, capital, approvals and delivery capability sitting with different parties. This page explains how a joint venture or partnership may apply, and what to settle early.

Discuss this sector ← All industries
How a partnership may apply

Where a joint venture may fit.

Real estate and infrastructure projects are usually long, capital-heavy and dependent on approvals. That is why parties sometimes combine resources: one may hold land or a site, another may bring planning, funding or construction capability, and a third may bring operating or financing expertise.

Infrastructure work adds further parties, such as public bodies, contractors and lenders, so roles and responsibilities need to be written down even more carefully. The right structure depends on the project, and a lawyer should advise on it.

General information

Possible opportunity types

  • Landowner and developer collaboration on a site
  • Redevelopment of an existing property
  • Commercial or mixed-use development partnerships
  • Collaboration between contractors, funders and promoters on a project
  • Joint ownership or operation of an asset once built

To be confirmed Business confirmation needed

Real Estate & Infrastructure is listed as a sector on this website, which notes that actual service coverage should be confirmed before publication. This page does not claim that Velan has completed projects, holds credentials or has specialist expertise in this sector.

Contributions

What partners may bring.

One party may contribute
  • Land, a site or an existing asset, with the documents that show ownership
  • Cooperation with surveys, approvals and paperwork
  • Capital or other resources, if agreed
Another party may contribute
  • Planning, design and project management
  • Construction capability and, possibly, some or all of the funding
  • Marketing, sales or operating capability, if agreed

Who contributes what differs from one arrangement to the next. It is settled between the parties and should be recorded in writing, not assumed.

Evaluation

Key questions to settle early.

  • What is being contributed by each party, and when?
  • Who applies for each approval and who bears delay or refusal?
  • How is the outcome shared, and on what assumptions?
  • Who funds cost overruns or further capital?
  • How are decisions made and recorded?
  • What are the milestones and what happens if they slip?
  • How are disputes, deadlock and exit handled?
  • Which checks need a lawyer, valuer or engineer?

Bring your answers to a consultation, or read the joint venture guide first.

Risks and practical points

Common risks and practical considerations.

Risk or consideration

Title and approvals

Ownership and permission issues can stop a project. They need verification by qualified professionals, not assumption.

Risk or consideration

Funding and cost

Costs and timelines can change. Agree who carries each risk and how extra funding is handled.

Risk or consideration

Unclear sharing terms

Quoted ratios vary and none is standard. Test any proposal against your own project.

Risk or consideration

Long timelines

Projects can run for years. Governance, reporting and exit terms matter more over time.

Home / Industries / Technology & Services
Industry perspective

Technology and services partnerships.

Innovation and strategic capability alignment often involve companies that are strong in different areas. This page explains how a joint venture or alliance may apply to technology and services, and which questions matter most.

Discuss this sector ← All industries
How a partnership may apply

Where a joint venture may fit.

Technology businesses sometimes team up because each side holds something the other lacks: a product, a customer base, engineering capacity, domain knowledge or a route to market. A partnership can range from a contract-based alliance to a jointly owned company.

What makes technology collaboration distinctive is that the main assets are intangible. Who owns the code, the data and the improvements made along the way is usually the hardest question, and it should be settled in writing before work begins.

General information

Possible opportunity types

  • Combining a product with a partner’s distribution or customer relationships
  • Co-developing a solution where each party brings different technical strength
  • Service delivery alliances that share capacity or specialists
  • A jointly owned company to pursue a defined opportunity
  • Integration or referral partnerships between complementary offerings

To be confirmed Business confirmation needed

Technology & Services is listed as a sector on this website, which notes that actual service coverage should be confirmed before publication. This page does not claim that Velan has completed projects, holds credentials or has specialist expertise in this sector.

Contributions

What partners may bring.

One party may contribute
  • A product, platform or technical know-how
  • Engineering or delivery capacity
  • Intellectual property it already owns, under agreed terms
Another party may contribute
  • Customer access, channels or market presence
  • Domain expertise or regulated-sector experience
  • Funding, infrastructure or support operations

Who contributes what differs from one arrangement to the next. It is settled between the parties and should be recorded in writing, not assumed.

Evaluation

Key questions to settle early.

  • Who owns existing intellectual property and who owns what is created together?
  • How is customer and personal data handled, stored and protected?
  • Who is responsible for support, maintenance and security?
  • What happens to the code and data if the partnership ends?
  • How are revenue, costs and credit shared?
  • Can either party work with competitors?
  • How are product decisions and roadmaps agreed?
  • Which technical or legal reviews are needed before launch?

Bring your answers to a consultation, or read the joint venture guide first.

Risks and practical points

Common risks and practical considerations.

Risk or consideration

Intellectual property

Unclear ownership of code, designs or improvements is a common source of dispute. Define it before development starts.

Risk or consideration

Data and privacy

Handling personal data brings legal duties. Take advice on data protection obligations that apply to your arrangement.

Risk or consideration

Dependence

One party may become reliant on the other’s platform or people. Plan for continuity and exit.

Risk or consideration

Pace and culture

Different working styles and release cycles can strain a partnership. Agree on how decisions and delivery are managed.

Industry perspective

Manufacturing joint ventures.

Capability, supply and production partnerships work best when plant, process, quality and market responsibilities are clear. This page explains how a joint venture may apply to manufacturing and what to check first.

Discuss this sector ← All industries
How a partnership may apply

Where a joint venture may fit.

Manufacturers may partner to share capacity, add a product line, enter a new market or secure supply. One party may bring a plant and process knowledge while another brings technology, brand, customers or capital.

Because production depends on physical assets and tight quality control, manufacturing partnerships need operational detail: who runs the plant, who sets quality standards, who buys the output and who carries the risk of idle capacity or defects.

General information

Possible opportunity types

  • Sharing or adding production capacity
  • Contract or co-manufacturing arrangements
  • Combining a technology owner with a manufacturer
  • Supply-chain collaboration with key suppliers or buyers
  • A jointly owned unit for a defined product or market

To be confirmed Business confirmation needed

Manufacturing is listed as a sector on this website, which notes that actual service coverage should be confirmed before publication. This page does not claim that Velan has completed projects, holds credentials or has specialist expertise in this sector.

Contributions

What partners may bring.

One party may contribute
  • A plant, equipment or production capacity
  • Process and operating know-how
  • Local workforce, suppliers or sites
Another party may contribute
  • Product technology, design or a brand
  • Customers, orders or distribution
  • Capital for equipment or expansion

Who contributes what differs from one arrangement to the next. It is settled between the parties and should be recorded in writing, not assumed.

Evaluation

Key questions to settle early.

  • Who owns and operates the equipment and premises?
  • Who sets and checks quality standards, and who bears defects or recalls?
  • How are raw materials sourced and priced?
  • What are minimum volumes and who carries idle capacity?
  • Who owns product designs, tooling and process know-how?
  • Which licences, standards and certifications apply to the product?
  • How are costs, margins and output shared?
  • How does the arrangement end and what happens to the assets?

Bring your answers to a consultation, or read the joint venture guide first.

Risks and practical points

Common risks and practical considerations.

Risk or consideration

Quality and compliance

Product standards, safety and environmental duties can differ by product. Check what applies and who is responsible.

Risk or consideration

Capacity and demand

Plans based on expected orders can fail if demand changes. Test assumptions and agree how shortfalls are handled.

Risk or consideration

Supply dependence

Reliance on one supplier or one customer concentrates risk. Plan alternatives.

Risk or consideration

Know-how leakage

Sharing process knowledge needs protection through confidentiality and clear ownership terms.

How a partnership may apply

Where a joint venture may fit.

Service businesses often grow by combining what they do well. A firm with strong delivery may partner with one that has client relationships, or two specialists may offer a joint solution neither could provide alone.

In services, the people are the product. That makes the key questions human ones: who holds the client relationship, who is accountable for the work, how are staff and reputation protected, and how is revenue divided.

General information

Possible opportunity types

Trade and distribution partnerships.

Market access and channel collaboration are the heart of trade. This page explains how a joint venture or distribution partnership may apply, and the commercial questions worth settling first.

Discuss this sector ← All industries
How a partnership may apply

Where a joint venture may fit.

Trading and distribution partnerships connect a product with a market. A producer may need reach, a distributor may want a product line, or two traders may pool buying power, warehousing or logistics to serve a wider area.

The agreement should answer practical questions: which territory and customers, whether the arrangement is exclusive, who holds stock and carries credit risk, and how pricing and returns work.

General information

Possible opportunity types

  • Distribution or dealership arrangements for a territory
  • Market entry with a local partner
  • Pooled warehousing, logistics or purchasing
  • Import and export collaboration
  • A jointly owned trading or distribution company

Contributions

  • A product, brand or supply source
  • Pricing support and product knowledge
  • Inventory or production capacity
Another party may contribute
  • Distribution network, customers or retail reach
  • Warehousing, logistics and local presence
  • Working capital and credit management

Who contributes what differs from one arrangement to the next. It is settled between the parties and should be recorded in writing, not assumed.

Risk or consideration

Compliance

Registrations, taxes and import-export rules may apply. Take professional advice on what is relevant to your goods.

Risk or consideration

Channel conflict

Selling through several routes can cause disputes. Define which customers and channels belong to whom.

Where a joint venture may fit.

Because the partners speak different commercial languages, clarity matters more. Terms, timelines, risk appetite and success measures should be put into plain words so that everyone is working from the same assumptions.

General information

An alliance is lighter and easier to leave. A joint venture involves more shared investment and control. The choice depends on the goal and the level of commitment.

With a clear statement of the objective and what each side can contribute. Then discuss structure, risk and professional checks.

How to Choose a Joint Venture Consultant in Chennai: 10 Questions to Ask

What to check, which questions to ask and how to prepare for a first discussion.

← All articles

Partnership StrategyPublication date to be addedGeneral information, not advice

A joint venture can bring businesses together around a shared opportunity. It can also create difficult questions about contributions, decisions, risk, and responsibilities. If you are exploring a joint venture in Chennai, the consultant you choose can influence how clearly you assess those questions before you commit.

This guide gives you 10 practical questions to ask before engaging a joint venture consultant. Use them to understand what the consultant actually does, how the work is scoped, and where you may need independent professional advice. Velan Joint Ventures works with businesses exploring partnerships, partner identification, feasibility, structuring, and property joint ventures. The right next step still depends on your goals and your specific project.

What does a joint venture consultant do?

A joint venture consultant helps you assess and organise a potential collaboration. Depending on the agreed scope, that work may include clarifying goals, defining partner criteria, reviewing feasibility questions, and coordinating discussions. A consultant does not automatically provide legal, tax, financial, engineering, or construction services. Ask what the consultant will deliver and which specialists you need.

A joint venture can take different forms. The parties might collaborate under a contract, form a separate company, or agree on another structure. The suitable arrangement depends on the objective, contributions, governance, liabilities, and other project details. India’s Companies Act provides a legal framework for companies, but a qualified lawyer should advise on the structure and documents for your particular arrangement. Official source: India Code (Companies Act, 2013).

A consultant should help you make the opportunity clearer. They should not promise that every discussion will produce a partner, approval, profit, or successful project. Before you begin, agree on the scope, information you need to share, expected deliverables, fees, and who will do each task.

How do you choose a joint venture consultant in Chennai?

Choose a consultant whose role matches your current need. Ask about relevant service scope, partner selection, conflicts of interest, fees, communication, and professional boundaries. Check verifiable business details and request written terms. If your project involves property, assess the site and proposed development separately with qualified legal, financial, and technical professionals.

Ask these 10 questions before you proceed:

1. What kind of joint venture work do you handle?

Ask whether the consultant focuses on business partnerships, property development, partner identification, feasibility, structuring discussions, or project coordination.

2. What would you do for my specific opportunity?

A clear answer should connect the work to your objective. Ask for the proposed scope in writing, including what the consultant will deliver and what falls outside it.

3. How do you identify or assess potential partners?

Ask what partner criteria they use, how they verify information, and whether you can review or approve a potential introduction before moving forward.

4. Who do you represent?

Find out whether the consultant represents you, the other party, both parties, or neither. Ask how they handle conflicts of interest and referral fees.

5. What information should I prepare?

A first discussion may need only a general description of your goals, location, approximate project size, and preferred collaboration. Ask before sharing confidential records.

6. How do you approach feasibility?

Ask which assumptions the consultant can help organise and which require specialist review. A feasibility discussion does not replace technical, legal, tax, planning, or financial advice.

7. How do you charge?

Request the fee basis, payment timing, taxes, expenses, and any success-based component in writing. Do not assume a consultation is free or that a quoted fee covers every stage.

8. How will you keep me informed?

Agree on a contact person, update frequency, decision points, and how the consultant will record questions and actions.

9. What happens if the opportunity is not suitable?

Ask how the engagement ends, what work you still receive, and whether any fees or obligations continue.

10. Which independent advisers should I involve?

Ask when to involve your own lawyer, accountant, property professional, engineer, or other specialist. Keep their role independent when you make consequential decisions.

These questions help you compare what a provider promises with what the written scope actually says. They also make it easier to see whether you need an adviser, a developer, or both. For a side-by-side look at Chennai providers, see our comparison of joint venture advisers and developers.

What should property owners check before a property joint venture?

Before discussing a property joint venture, clarify the land details, your goals, the proposed development, each party’s responsibilities, and the assumptions behind any sharing proposal. Verify ownership and project information through appropriate records and independent professionals. Do not treat a headline ratio, verbal assurance, or preliminary estimate as a final agreement.

For a property opportunity, prepare a simple outline:

  • The area and general location of the land.
  • The approximate plot size and current use.
  • Your preferred outcome, such as residential, commercial, or another use.
  • Your questions about contributions, approvals, design, construction, timelines, and allocation.
  • Any known constraints, without sending sensitive title or financial documents through an unverified channel.

Then ask the consultant how they would help you evaluate the next step. They may help organise partner criteria, identify questions for discussion, or coordinate inputs. They should explain clearly when another professional needs to verify a document or give formal advice.

Do not assume that one sharing ratio applies across Chennai or across projects. The commercial terms depend on the land, project assumptions, contributions, responsibilities, costs, approvals, and negotiated agreement. Ask each party to explain its proposal and record the assumptions behind it.

If a project or promoter is subject to registration requirements, verify the relevant details through the appropriate authority. For Tamil Nadu projects, start with the Tamil Nadu Real Estate Regulatory Authority. A portal lookup does not replace independent title, legal, planning, or technical review.

You can also check official company or LLP details using the Ministry of Corporate Affairs master-data services. The MCA explains that the public can access company and LLP master data through its portal.

How much does a joint venture consultant in Chennai cost?

Fees depend on the provider, project, and agreed scope. Ask for a written proposal that separates consultation, research, partner identification, coordination, and any success-based charges. Confirm taxes, expenses, payment milestones, exclusions, and termination terms. Compare the work included, not just the headline fee.

Before you accept a proposal, check whether the fee covers one discussion or ongoing support. Ask whether the consultant charges for travel, document review, third-party specialists, introductions, or project coordination. If the provider proposes a success fee, clarify how they define success and when the fee becomes due.

A written scope should tell you what the consultant will do, what you must provide, and what the provider cannot guarantee. It should also explain how either party can pause or end the engagement. If you cannot understand a fee clause, ask for clarification before you sign.

No consultant can guarantee that a partner will accept your proposal or that a project will receive approvals, reach a particular value, or deliver a specific return. Treat guaranteed outcomes as a reason to ask more questions.

How is a consultant different from a builder?

A consultant may help you assess an opportunity, organise partner criteria, and coordinate discussions. A builder or developer may propose to plan or execute construction. Some companies combine roles. Ask who each party represents, who controls the work, who bears each cost, and who remains accountable under the agreement.

A builder may be the right contact when you already know the project and want to discuss execution. An adviser may help earlier, when you need to compare options, test assumptions, or clarify what kind of partner you need. Some providers offer both advisory and development services, so ask about their incentives and responsibilities.

In a property joint venture, list who handles land, funding, planning, approvals, design, construction, marketing, sales, maintenance, and handover. Have qualified professionals review the relevant documents. This article provides general information, not legal, tax, investment, or construction advice.

Where Velan Joint Ventures fits

For property joint ventures, start with a general discussion of the opportunity and the questions you want to resolve.

Velan does not guarantee a partner match, project approval, sharing ratio, profit, or business result. Confirm the proposed service scope, fees, and next steps before you engage.

The bottom line

Choose a joint venture consultant by the work they can clearly explain and the boundaries they respect. Ask about scope, partner selection, fees, conflicts, communication, and independent professional review.

Prepare your goals and questions before the first discussion. A clear process can help you decide what to investigate next, even when you decide not to proceed.

To explore the topic further, read Velan’s property joint venture guide, Chennai overview, services, and contact page. To discuss an opportunity, call +91 96264 12116 or email velanpropertydevelopers@gmail.com.

Partnership Strategy

What should businesses clarify before entering a joint venture?

A practical overview of objectives, contributions, governance, responsibilities and exit considerations.

← All articles

Partnership StrategyPublication date to be addedGeneral information, not advice

Most joint venture disagreements trace back to questions that were never asked in the early conversations. Before term sheets and agreements, it helps to write down, together, what each party wants, what it will contribute and what success means.

  • Objectives: why each party is entering, and whether those goals are compatible.
  • Contributions: capital, people, assets, intellectual property, customer access or licences, and how each is valued.
  • Roles and responsibilities: who runs day-to-day operations and who is accountable for what.
  • Governance: how decisions are made, which matters need every party's approval, and how deadlocks are handled.
  • Economics: how costs, profits and losses are shared.
  • Exit: what happens if goals change, a party wants out, or the venture comes to an end.

Clarifying these points early does not remove risk, but it turns hidden assumptions into explicit discussion points that legal, tax and financial advisers can then reflect in formal documents.

General information only. It is not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Partnership Strategy

How to assess strategic fit in a potential business partner

Questions to help compare capabilities, expectations, operating styles and long-term goals.

← All articles

Partnership StrategyPublication date to be addedGeneral information, not advice

A partner can look strong on paper and still be a poor fit. Strategic fit is about whether two organisations can actually work together towards the same outcome.

  • Capability fit: does the partner bring what you lack, and do you bring what they lack?
  • Goal alignment: are time horizons, growth ambitions and appetite for risk compatible?
  • Operating style: decision speed, reporting habits, and approach to quality and compliance.
  • Reputation and track record: verified through references and public records.
  • Resource commitment: will the partner genuinely assign people and attention?
  • Culture and communication: how disagreements are likely to be handled.

A simple weighted scorecard, agreed before you meet candidates, helps compare options consistently and reduces the pull of first impressions.

General information only. It is not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Deal Structures

Contractual vs equity joint ventures: choosing a structure

How collaboration under a contract differs from creating a jointly owned entity, and what to weigh.

← All articles

Deal StructuresPublication date to be addedGeneral information, not advice

“Joint venture” describes a purpose, not a single legal form. Broadly, parties either collaborate under a contract, or create a separate entity that they jointly own.

  • Contractual collaboration: the parties stay separate and agree roles, sharing and duration by contract. This is often quicker to set up and easier to unwind; control and liability sit with each party.
  • Equity joint venture: a new entity is formed with shared ownership. It gives assets, people and contracts a clear home, but brings governance, reporting and exit mechanics to design.
  • Factors that influence the choice: duration, scale of investment, regulatory requirements, tax treatment, liability, and the need to ring-fence the activity.

The right structure depends on jurisdiction and circumstances. Entity form, tax and regulatory treatment should be confirmed with qualified legal and tax professionals.

General information only. It is not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Deal Structures

Governance and decision rights in a joint venture

Who decides what, and what happens when the parties disagree? Points to settle before launch.

← All articles

Deal StructuresPublication date to be addedGeneral information, not advice

Governance determines who decides what, and what happens when the parties disagree. Settling it before launch is far easier than negotiating it in the middle of a dispute.

  • Board or steering committee composition and meeting rhythm.
  • Reserved matters: decisions that need approval from every party, such as budgets, new borrowing, major contracts or changes in scope.
  • Management roles and reporting lines.
  • Information rights and reporting standards.
  • Deadlock procedures: escalation, mediation or structured exit routes.
  • Funding calls: how extra capital is requested and what happens if a party cannot contribute.

These are commercial discussion points to agree between the parties. Formal drafting belongs with legal counsel.

General information only. It is not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Home / Blogs / Building a joint venture risk register
Risk Management

Building a joint venture risk register

Turn vague concerns into trackable items with owners, early-warning signs and agreed responses.

← All articles

Risk ManagementPublication date to be addedGeneral information, not advice

A risk register turns vague concerns into trackable items with owners. It is one of the simplest tools for keeping a partnership on course.

  • Strategic: goals drift apart or the market shifts.
  • Commercial: demand, pricing or customer assumptions prove wrong.
  • Operational: capacity, quality or delivery problems.
  • Legal and regulatory: licences, compliance and contractual obligations.
  • Financial: funding gaps, cost overruns and cash-flow timing.
  • People and culture: key-person dependency and misaligned working styles.
  • Reputational: one party's actions affecting the other.
  • Exit: difficulty unwinding or valuing the venture.

For each risk, record likelihood, impact, an owner, an early-warning indicator and the agreed response. Review the register at every governance meeting.

General information only. It is not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Risk Management

Due diligence for partner evaluation: what to organise

How to test what a prospective partner tells you, and how to coordinate specialist reviews.

← All articles

Risk ManagementPublication date to be addedGeneral information, not advice

Due diligence is how you test what a prospective partner tells you. The scope should match the size and risk of the venture.

  • Corporate: ownership, authority to enter the venture and group structure.
  • Financial: statements, obligations and funding capacity, reviewed by qualified accountants.
  • Legal: litigation, licences, intellectual property ownership and key contracts.
  • Commercial: customers, suppliers and market position.
  • Operational and technical: capabilities, facilities and systems.
  • Compliance and reputation: regulatory standing, references and public record.

A coordinator can help organise requests and findings so specialist advisers see consistent information. The professional opinions themselves must come from appropriately qualified specialists.

General information only. It is not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Home / Blogs / Reading market signals before you partner
Market Trends

Reading market signals before you partner

A simple framework for turning market trends into testable assumptions rather than conclusions.

← All articles

Market TrendsPublication date to be addedGeneral information, not advice

Partnerships are often prompted by market shifts, but a trend is only useful if you can tie it to a decision. Treat market signals as inputs to a hypothesis, not as proof.

  • Define the question: what would you do differently if the signal is real?
  • Prefer primary sources: regulators, industry bodies, audited filings and direct customer conversations.
  • Separate signal from noise: check how recent, how large and how well sourced the evidence is.
  • Test the assumption: what must be true for the partnership to make sense, and how will you check it?
  • Revisit: set dates to re-test the assumptions.

This page does not publish market statistics. When verified, sourced market data is available it will be added with its source and review date.

General information only. It is not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Industry Benchmarks

Which benchmarks matter when evaluating a joint venture?

How to choose, check and use industry benchmarks without over-trusting a single number.

← All articles

Industry BenchmarksPublication date to be addedGeneral information, not advice

Benchmarks help you judge whether a venture's assumptions are realistic, but only if they are comparable and current.

  • Tie benchmarks to the decision: for example margins, utilisation, acquisition cost or time to break-even, as relevant to the sector.
  • Check comparability: size, geography, business model and time period.
  • Prefer documented sources and note the date.
  • Use ranges rather than single numbers, and show your own assumptions beside them.
  • Record what you could not benchmark.

No benchmark figures are published here yet. A verified industry benchmarks report appears in the resource plan further down this page.

How to read a joint venture case study critically

What makes a success story credible, and what to look for before relying on one.

← All articles

Success StoriesPublication date to be addedGeneral information, not advice

Case studies are persuasive, so it pays to read them critically, whether they come from an adviser, a partner or your own team.

  • Is the situation described specifically, including the constraints?
  • Are results attributable, measured and dated, or merely asserted?
  • Were challenges and trade-offs included?
  • Did the parties consent to being named, and can the claims be verified?
  • How similar is the context to yours?

Home / Insights / Joint venture guide
Joint venture guide

Joint venture meaning: types, benefits and risks.

A plain guide to what a joint venture is, the two main structures, why businesses consider them, what can go wrong and what to settle first. General information only, not legal, tax or investment advice.

Discuss a joint venture Read the FAQs
Meaning

What is a joint venture?

A joint venture (JV) is an arrangement in which two or more independent businesses combine resources, capital or expertise to pursue a shared objective. The businesses stay separate organisations. They may run the venture through a contract alone, or choose to form a separate legal entity for it.

Joint ventures are usually built around a defined project, market or purpose rather than the whole of each business. The agreed terms, not the label, decide how control, cost, profit and exit work.

In one line

Separate businesses, one shared objective

The Oxford Advanced Learner’s Dictionary describes a joint venture as a business project or activity begun by two or more companies that remain separate organisations.

Source: Oxford Learner’s Dictionaries

Example from India, for illustration only. Tata Consumer Products describes Tata Starbucks as a joint venture between Starbucks Coffee Company and Tata Consumer Products Limited (Tata Consumer Products). Velan Joint Ventures has no connection with this venture, and the example says nothing about how it is structured.

Structures

Incorporated and unincorporated joint ventures.

Incorporated (equity)

A separate legal entity

  • The partners set up a separate entity and hold ownership in it
  • In India a company is a common route, formed under the Companies Act, 2013; other entity forms may also be possible
  • Ownership, board control and shareholder rights are usually set out in the constitutional documents and a shareholders’ agreement
  • Often considered for longer-term or larger ventures
Unincorporated (contractual)

An agreement between the partners

  • The partners agree terms by contract and do not create a new entity
  • In India a contract is an agreement enforceable by law (Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 2(h))
  • Often considered for a defined project, research effort or time-limited collaboration
  • Roles, sharing, liability and exit depend entirely on what the contract says

The better choice depends on the objective, the length of the collaboration, the risks, the tax position and the partners’ preferences. Liability, control and tax consequences differ, so choose the structure with a qualified lawyer and tax adviser. Sources: Companies Act, 2013 (India Code) and Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 2(h).

Why parties consider them

Possible purposes and benefits.

Market access

New markets or customers

A partner with local knowledge, relationships or distribution may help a business reach a market it would find hard to enter alone.

Cost and risk

Sharing the load

Large projects can need more capital or carry more risk than one party wants to hold. A venture can spread both, depending on the terms.

Capabilities

Pooling complementary skills

One party may bring technology, land or capital and another may bring operations, access or experience.

These are possibilities, not promises. Whether a venture delivers them depends on the partners, the terms and the market.

What to weigh

Common risks and challenges.

People and direction
  • Management conflict and unclear decision rights
  • Cultural or strategic misalignment between the partners
  • Governance gaps: who decides, who reports, how often
Information and money
  • Exposure of intellectual property or sensitive information to a partner
  • Different expectations about profit, timing and further funding
  • Exit disputes when there is no agreed way out

Many of these can be reduced by discussing them early and writing the answers down. Velan’s due diligence coordination and structuring support are aimed at these points.

Before you start

Questions to settle before any agreement.

  • What exactly is the shared objective, and how will we know it is met?
  • What does each party contribute (money, land, people, technology, access) and when?
  • Who makes which decisions, and what needs both parties’ consent?
  • How are profit, losses and further funding shared?
  • How are confidential information and intellectual property protected?
  • How are disagreements handled before they become disputes?
  • What approvals or licences are needed, and who obtains them?
  • How can a party exit, and what happens to the venture then?

General information Not legal, tax or investment advice

Laws and rules change and differ by sector. Competition, foreign investment, tax and sector-specific rules may apply to your venture. Confirm them with qualified professionals before committing.

Frequently asked questions

Joint venture questions.

General information, not legal, tax or investment advice.

A joint venture is a business project or activity begun by two or more companies that remain separate organisations. The parties combine resources, capital or expertise for a shared objective and agree how control, costs and outcomes are shared.

An incorporated (equity) joint venture is run through a separate legal entity that the partners own. An unincorporated (contractual) joint venture is based on a contract between the partners and does not create a new entity. Each has different consequences for liability, control, tax and exit, so take legal and tax advice before choosing.

Not necessarily. “Joint venture” describes a commercial arrangement, usually around a specific project or objective, while “partnership” has a specific legal meaning under Indian law. How an arrangement is treated depends on its terms and the law, so ask a qualified lawyer about your case.

No. A joint venture can open possibilities such as new markets, shared costs and complementary skills, but results depend on the partners, the terms and the market. Nothing on this website promises an outcome.

Common points include each party’s contribution, decision rights, how profit and losses are shared, how information and intellectual property are protected, how disputes are handled and how a party can exit. A lawyer should draft and review the agreement.

Velan helps organise the commercial discussion through its structuring support. Drafting and review of the agreement should be done by qualified legal professionals.

Home / Services / Joint Venture Advisory
01 / Advisory

Joint venture advisory for considered partnerships.

Clarify objectives, explore collaboration models and assess how a potential joint venture could support your business strategy.

Discuss this service Read the FAQs
Joint Venture Advisory

What this service is and why it matters.

A joint venture is one way for two or more parties to pursue a defined business objective together while agreeing how resources, control and returns are shared. It is rarely the only option. Joint venture advisory starts with a plain question: is collaboration the right route, and if so, which model fits? That might be a contractual arrangement, a jointly owned entity, a project-specific alliance or something lighter.

Velan Joint Ventures offers this as a conversation-led service. The aim is to put your objective, what each side could contribute and the questions that need specialist input in one place, so later steps such as partner search, feasibility, structuring and diligence rest on a shared understanding. Legal, tax and financial advice stays with qualified professionals.

At a glance

Good fit if…

  • You are considering a collaboration but have not settled on a model.
  • You already have a possible partner and want to test the fit.
  • You want a structured way to prepare before approaching legal or financial advisers.

Helpful to bring

  • A short description of your business and the opportunity
  • What you can contribute and what you are looking for
  • Your timeline and any constraints
Scope

What the work can include.

  • Discussion of your objective and strategic fit
  • Comparison of collaboration models for your situation
  • Evaluation criteria for a potential partner
  • A list of open questions and who should answer them
  • Suggested next steps and their sequence

Scope is agreed per engagement. This page is general information and not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Questions we work through
  • What do we want from this collaboration that we cannot achieve alone?
  • What could each party contribute: capital, land, capability, customers, people?
  • Who decides what, and how are disagreements resolved?
  • How long is the collaboration meant to run, and what happens at the end?
  • Which risks need legal, tax or financial review before we go further?

Home / Services / Strategic Partner Identification
02 / Connections

Strategic partner identification built on clear criteria.

Define the partner profile, capabilities and alignment criteria relevant to your business opportunity.

Discuss this service Read the FAQs
Strategic Partner Identification

What this service is and why it matters.

Finding a joint venture partner is less about a long list of names and more about a clear description of who would actually fit. Capabilities, resources, operating style, expectations about control and the time each side can commit all shape whether a partnership holds together after the first few months.

Partner identification at Velan Joint Ventures begins by writing that profile down. From there, candidates can be considered against the criteria you agree, depending on the opportunity, the target profile, the network available and the scope you agree. No partner match or outcome is guaranteed.

At a glance

Good fit if…

  • You know what you need but not who could provide it.
  • You have several possible partners and need a fair way to compare them.
  • You want clear criteria before you approach anyone.

Helpful to bring

  • The capabilities or access you are looking for
  • Any partners already in mind, and why
  • Deal-breakers on either side
Scope

What the work can include.

  • A written partner profile and must-have versus nice-to-have criteria
  • Alignment criteria covering capability, resources and expectations
  • A framework to compare candidates consistently
  • Suggested questions for first conversations
  • Hand-off to feasibility and diligence when you are ready

Scope is agreed per engagement. This page is general information and not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Questions we work through
  • Which capability or access are we missing, and who holds it?
  • Do the parties want the same level of involvement and control?
  • Are the timelines and financial expectations compatible?
  • What would make a partner a poor fit even if the numbers work?
  • How will we verify what a candidate tells us?

Home / Services / Feasibility & Opportunity Assessment
03 / Evaluation

Feasibility and opportunity assessment before you commit.

Explore market context, strategic fit, assumptions, resource needs and key questions before moving ahead.

Discuss this service Read the FAQs
Feasibility & Opportunity Assessment

What this service is and why it matters.

Most joint venture problems trace back to assumptions that were never written down: how fast revenue would ramp up, what each side would spend, how long approvals would take. A feasibility assessment makes those assumptions visible while changing course is still cheap.

At Velan Joint Ventures this means walking through market context, strategic fit, resource needs and dependencies, and listing the questions that need specialist review. You can also test your own numbers in the ROI estimator on the Insights page, which shows its assumptions on screen.

At a glance

Good fit if…

  • You have an opportunity but have not tested the numbers or the dependencies.
  • You need to explain the opportunity to internal stakeholders.
  • You want to compare two or more options on the same basis.

Helpful to bring

  • Any figures or projections you already have
  • The decision you need to make, and by when
  • Known constraints (budget, approvals, people)
Scope

What the work can include.

  • Market context and strategic-fit discussion
  • An assumptions list, with owners for each assumption
  • Resource and dependency mapping
  • Key questions for legal, finance or technical specialists
  • A go, adjust or pause view for your own decision

Scope is agreed per engagement. This page is general information and not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Questions we work through
  • Which three assumptions would hurt most if they were wrong?
  • What must be in place (approvals, people, funding) before work starts?
  • What does a realistic ramp-up look like, and who pays for it?
  • What would we do if the first year runs behind plan?
  • Which questions can only a specialist answer?

Home / Services / Due Diligence Coordination
04 / Risk review

Due diligence coordination for partner evaluation.

Help organise partner evaluation and coordinate relevant information with qualified legal, finance and technical professionals.

Discuss this service Read the FAQs
Due Diligence Coordination

What this service is and why it matters.

Due diligence is the work of checking what you have been told. For a joint venture that can cover the partner itself, the asset or project being contributed, and the assumptions behind the plan. Each strand needs a qualified specialist, and the strands need to be kept in step with each other.

Velan Joint Ventures focuses on coordination: organising the evaluation, deciding what needs checking, gathering the relevant information and keeping legal, finance and technical reviewers working from the same list. Velan does not replace those professionals and this service is not legal, tax or financial advice.

At a glance

Good fit if…

  • You have shortlisted a partner and need a disciplined way to check them.
  • Several advisers are involved and you want one point of coordination.
  • You want a record of what was checked and what remains open.

Helpful to bring

  • The partner or project under evaluation
  • Advisers you already work with, if any
  • What has been shared so far, and under what terms
Scope

What the work can include.

  • A diligence checklist matched to your opportunity
  • Allocation of each item to the right professional
  • Tracking of information requests and open points
  • A consolidated summary of findings for your decision
  • Links into structuring discussions once points are resolved

Scope is agreed per engagement. This page is general information and not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Questions we work through
  • What would change our decision if we found it was untrue?
  • Who is qualified to verify each claim?
  • What information does each side need to share, and under what confidentiality?
  • Which findings are deal-breakers and which can be managed?
  • How will open points be tracked to closure?

Home / Services / JV Structuring Support
05 / Structure

Joint venture agreement and structuring support.

Map key commercial discussion points such as contributions, governance, responsibilities, decision rights and exit considerations.

Discuss this service Read the FAQs
JV Structuring Support

What this service is and why it matters.

A joint venture agreement records what the parties have already agreed in principle. The harder, earlier work is getting to that agreement: who contributes what, who decides what, how profits and losses are shared, what happens if a party wants out. Structuring support helps you lay those commercial points out clearly before they are drafted.

Velan Joint Ventures helps organise the commercial discussion points and the choices between structures, for example a contractual arrangement compared with a jointly owned entity. Drafting, review and advice on the agreement itself should be undertaken by appropriately qualified legal professionals.

At a glance

Good fit if…

  • You agree on the idea and need to turn it into specific commercial terms.
  • You are comparing structures before instructing lawyers.
  • You want both parties to see the same list of points.

Helpful to bring

  • The parties and what each will contribute
  • Any principles already agreed
  • Which advisers will draft and review
Scope

What the work can include.

  • A term-sheet style list of commercial points to settle
  • Discussion of contributions, governance and decision rights
  • Responsibilities and reporting between the parties
  • Exit, deadlock and dispute-resolution considerations to raise with counsel
  • Coordination with legal and tax advisers on the chosen structure

Scope is agreed per engagement. This page is general information and not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Questions we work through
  • Is a contract enough, or does this need a separate jointly owned entity?
  • How are contributions valued, and what happens if one side contributes late?
  • Which decisions need both parties, and which can be delegated?
  • How are profits, losses and further funding handled?
  • What are the exit routes, and how is a deadlock broken?

06 / Execution

Project and collaboration coordination through agreed stages.

Support stakeholder alignment, action tracking and communication through agreed stages of a collaboration.

Discuss this service Read the FAQs
Project & Collaboration Coordination

What this service is and why it matters.

Once a collaboration has started, the common failure is not disagreement but drift: actions without owners, decisions nobody recorded, two teams working to different versions of the plan. Coordination keeps the agreed stages visible and the people involved informed.

Velan Joint Ventures supports stakeholder alignment, action tracking and communication through the stages you agree. The scope is set at the start, and it remains your collaboration: decisions belong to the parties involved.

At a glance

Good fit if…

  • A collaboration is starting and you want a clear rhythm from day one.
  • Several stakeholders need to stay aligned.
  • You want actions and decisions recorded in one place.

Helpful to bring

  • The agreed stages or milestones
  • The people involved on each side
  • How progress is reported today
Scope

What the work can include.

  • A shared action and decision log
  • Regular stakeholder check-ins at agreed intervals
  • Communication between parties on open points
  • Tracking of agreed milestones
  • Escalation of items to the right decision-maker

Scope is agreed per engagement. This page is general information and not legal, tax, financial or investment advice.

Questions we work through
  • Who owns each action, and by when?
  • How are decisions recorded and communicated?
  • How often do the parties meet, and who attends?
  • What triggers an escalation?
  • When do we review whether the collaboration is meeting its objectives?

Home / Services / Property joint ventures
Real estate & infrastructure

Property joint ventures and development partnerships.

How a real estate joint venture or property development joint venture works, what the parties usually need to settle, and where Velan Joint Ventures can help organise the discussion.

Discuss a property opportunity Read the FAQs
Real estate joint venture

What a property joint venture involves.

In property, a joint venture usually brings together a party that holds land or an existing asset and a party that brings development capability, funding or both. In India this is often documented as a joint development agreement. The parties agree what each contributes and how the outcome is shared: commonly either by sharing the built area or by sharing revenue from the project, though other arrangements exist.

The commercial structure matters as much as the idea. A contract between the parties and a separate jointly owned entity carry different consequences for liability, control and tax, and the right choice needs professional advice.

General information

Typical points to settle

  • What each party contributes and when
  • How the outcome is shared (area, revenue or another basis)
  • Approvals and who is responsible for obtaining them
  • Timeline, milestones and what happens if they slip
  • Cost overruns, further funding and decision rights
  • Exit, deadlock and dispute resolution

To be confirmed Business confirmation needed

Real estate and infrastructure is listed as a sector on this website (“project collaboration and development opportunities”), with a note that actual service coverage should be confirmed before publication. This page does not state which property mandates, locations or project types Velan takes on.

Roles

Landowner and developer roles, in general terms.

A landowner may contribute
  • The land or site, with the title documents needed to show ownership
  • Cooperation with approvals, surveys and paperwork
  • Possibly capital or other resources, if agreed
A developer may contribute
  • Planning, design and project management
  • Construction and, possibly, some or all of the funding
  • Applications for approvals, marketing and sales, if agreed

Who funds what and who does what differs from project to project. It is settled in the agreement between the parties and should never be assumed. A landowner does not always contribute no construction capital, and a developer does not always fund every cost.

Sharing terms

How the outcome is shared is negotiated.

The parties may share built area, revenue or another measure. The split depends on the site, the project, what each side contributes, the approvals, the market at the time and the agreement they negotiate.

You may see ratios quoted online or by builders. None is standard or guaranteed, and a figure that suits one site may not suit another. Treat any ratio as a starting point for discussion and have a lawyer and valuer test it against your own project.

Why no ratio is shown Not verified

This website does not quote a sharing ratio because Velan has no verified basis for presenting one as typical. Any example you see elsewhere is illustrative only.

Chennai

Approvals and rules to check in Chennai.

Planning permission

CMDA, within the Chennai Metropolitan Area

The Chennai Metropolitan Development Authority states that you must obtain planning permission from it before undertaking development in the Chennai Metropolitan Area. Whether your site falls inside that area, or under another planning authority, needs to be confirmed. CMDA: planning permission

RERA

Project registration

The Tamil Nadu Real Estate Regulatory Authority states that registration of real estate projects is mandatory, and describes the rules as covering projects with land over 500 square metres or more than eight apartments, counting all phases. Smaller projects may be exempt. TNRERA · MoHUA RERA FAQ

Title

Proof of ownership

CMDA’s FAQ lists documents such as a sale deed or lease deed and patta to establish title to the land when applying. Title checks should be done by a qualified lawyer. CMDA: FAQ

These pages were checked on 5 November 2026. Rules change and apply differently to each project, so confirm the current position with the authority and a qualified professional. The CMDA and TNRERA pages did not address joint development agreements specifically.

Before you discuss

Questions for a landowner or business to consider.

  • Where is the land, how large is it and what is its current use?
  • What kind of project is being considered: residential, commercial or mixed?
  • Who is responsible for each task, from design to construction to sales?
  • Which approvals are needed, who applies for them and who bears delay or refusal?
  • How is the project funded, and what if costs or timelines change?
  • How are decisions made, and what needs the landowner’s consent?
  • How are risks allocated between the parties?
  • What are the exit, deadlock and dispute terms?

Bring your answers to a consultation, or read the joint venture guide first. See also joint ventures in Chennai and JV structuring support.

Scope

Where Velan can help, and where it cannot.

Can help organise
  • Clarifying objectives and the right collaboration model (advisory)
  • Defining the kind of partner you need (partner identification)
  • Listing assumptions, resources and dependencies (feasibility)
  • Coordinating checks with qualified professionals (due diligence)
  • Mapping contributions, governance and exit points (structuring)
Needs qualified professionals
  • Title verification and legal due diligence
  • Drafting and reviewing the joint development or joint venture agreement
  • Tax advice and valuation
  • Regulatory registration and approvals
  • Engineering, planning and cost review

Velan coordinates the discussion; it does not replace these professionals, and no outcome is guaranteed.

Frequently asked questions

Property joint venture questions.

General information, not legal, tax or investment advice.

It is an arrangement where two or more parties combine land, capital, capability or other resources to carry out a property project and share the result on an agreed basis.

A property development joint venture is a real estate joint venture aimed at building or redeveloping property, often between a landowner and a developer. The parties agree contributions, timelines, approvals and how the outcome is shared.

Under area sharing the parties receive an agreed portion of the built area. Under revenue sharing they share sales or lease income from the project. Each has different risk, tax and cash-flow consequences, so take professional advice.

Commercial points can be organised through the structuring service. Drafting and review of the agreement should be done by qualified legal professionals.

This is to be confirmed by the business. Use the booking form to ask about your project and location.

No. Ratios quoted online vary and none is standard or guaranteed. The split depends on the site, the project, each party’s contributions, approvals, the market and what is negotiated. Illustrative figures should be tested by a lawyer and valuer against your own project.

No. Who funds construction and other costs is agreed case by case. Some arrangements have the developer funding most costs, but this should never be assumed. Confirm each party’s funding in writing.

No. Approvals come from the relevant authorities, and timelines, costs and outcomes can change. A joint venture agreement should say who is responsible for each step and what happens if it is delayed or refused.

CMDA states that planning permission is required before development in the Chennai Metropolitan Area, and TNRERA states that registration of real estate projects is mandatory under its rules, with smaller projects possibly exempt. Which apply to your site must be confirmed with the authority and a qualified professional.

Gather the title documents, the exact location and size of the land, how it is used now and what you want from the project. Then think through responsibilities, funding, approvals, decision rights, risk and exit. The questions above are a starting list.

This website presents Velan as a joint venture advisory business. Whether Velan undertakes construction or development itself is to be confirmed by the business. Please ask when you enquire.

If you have a specific opportunity, feasibility assessment tests the assumptions before you commit time and money.

New to joint ventures? Start with the joint venture guide. Searching for a joint venture consultant in Chennai? Velan lists its office in West Mambalam. See the Chennai hub and the service-areas index; area coverage beyond West Mambalam is to be confirmed by the business.

Transparency

Which features are live, and what each still needs.

Some features need a backend, a hosting setting or a third-party account. They are labelled honestly here rather than simulated.

Feature status and requirements
FeatureStatus in this fileWhat is needed to go live
Live chatNot connectedA live-chat provider and staff to answer. Set chatScriptUrl (https). Loads only after visitor consent.
AI chatbotNot connectedAn AI/chatbot service with approved answers, a privacy notice and safeguards. Nothing is simulated here.
FAQ finderWorking in the browserNothing needed. It searches this site’s FAQs locally; it is not AI and nothing is sent.
Appointment schedulingRequest form onlyA scheduling service (Calendly, Cal.com, Google Calendar appointment pages) set in booking, or a backend.
Client portal loginNot availableAn authentication provider, a database and a portal application. Set portalUrl when one exists.
Push notificationsNot availableHTTPS hosting, a service worker, a push service, a subscription store and explicit consent.
Video testimonialsPlaceholderReal, written-approval client videos with captions. Set aboutVideoEmbed for the About video.
Trust badgesPlaceholder slotsVerified registrations or memberships, with proof, supplied by the business.
Language supportEnglish onlyProfessionally reviewed translations. The language switch and data-i18n hooks are ready.
Currency and regionWorking (formatting only)Nothing needed. It changes number and currency formatting in the ROI estimator; no conversion is made.
ROI calculatorWorking in the browserNothing needed. See the Insights page for inputs, outputs and assumptions.
Case study filterWorking, sample contentApproved, verifiable case studies to replace the illustrative cards.
Accessibility controlsWorking in the browserHigh contrast, larger text and reduced motion, via the preferences dialog.
Lead scoringLocal scaffold, consent onlyA CRM or backend to store and act on scores. Here it runs in the browser tab only and sends nothing.
Analytics eventsConsent-gated data layerGoogle Tag Manager, GA4 or similar, installed after consent and a privacy notice.
Heatmaps and behaviour analyticsNot installedA heatmap provider. Set heatmapScriptUrl (https). Loads only after consent. Mask form fields.
Backup and recoveryDeployment taskHosting backups, version control and a restore test. Not something an HTML file can do.
